items.plain: Anything imperfect either advances or slips back, and if you ease off, you lose ground you can't simply resume. So keep going: most of the road lies ahead, but wanting to progress is most of progress.
items.core_idea: Wanting to progress is the greater part of progress

items.plain: We should make all our time our own, but that can only happen once we first belong to ourselves.
items.core_idea: To own your time, first own yourself

items.plain: When will we master our passions and be able to say we have won? The victory is not over foreign armies but over greed, ambition, and the fear of death, which have beaten even world conquerors.
items.core_idea: True conquest is over greed, ambition and fear of death

items.plain: Busy affairs that eat our time should be pushed aside, not patiently sorted out. Any time is right for useful study, yet many people neglect it in exactly the situations that make it necessary.
items.core_idea: Busyness is no excuse to neglect wisdom

items.plain: Those still short of wisdom can have their happiness broken, but the wise person's joy is like woven cloth no chance can tear. It depends on nothing outside; it is born within and stays there.
items.core_idea: The wise person's joy comes from within

items.plain: A healthy mind is content with itself, trusts itself, and sees that everything people pray for doesn't matter to a happy life. What can be added to or lost is not lasting; Fortune gives us nothing we truly own.
items.core_idea: Lasting happiness rests only on what is truly yours

items.plain: Like a dog snapping at scraps and gulping each one while waiting for more, we bolt whatever Fortune throws us without real pleasure. The wise person is satisfied and sets aside whatever comes to him.
items.core_idea: Greedy grasping brings no pleasure; the wise are satisfied

items.plain: Ambitious people never think of all those they have passed, only of those still ahead, and that bothers them more. Every craving is like this: it starts exactly where it ought to stop.
items.core_idea: Craving always begins where it should end

items.plain: I owe a great deal to the sun, the moon, the seasons and the god who rules them, even though none of them exists for me alone.
items.core_idea: We owe thanks even for gifts shared by all

items.plain: God comes not only near people but into them; no mind without God is good. Divine seeds are scattered in our bodies: a good cultivator grows them into something like their source, a bad one lets weeds take over.
items.core_idea: Divine seeds in us grow or die by our care

items.plain: People suffer over children, love and elections, but the largest crowd of the unhappy despair at the expectation of death, which can come from anywhere. Until you lose that fear, you live with a pounding heart.
items.core_idea: Fear of death makes the most people miserable

items.plain: We flinch at our neighbours' troubles like birds at the whirr of an empty sling. No one who yields to such fancies can be happy, for happiness needs calm, and a life of dread is poor.
items.core_idea: Happiness requires calm, not constant dread

items.plain: Whoever hands himself to Fortune is caught in a web of worry. The only way out is to scorn outside things and be content with what is honourable; whoever values anything above virtue waits anxiously on Fortune.
items.core_idea: Only valuing virtue frees you from Fortune's web

items.plain: Virtue needs nothing because it is pleased with what it has and does not crave what it lacks. To virtue, whatever is enough is plenty.
items.core_idea: Whatever is enough is abundance

items.plain: Trust fleeting goods and you soon lose them, and you suffer trying not to. Few people get to set prosperity down gently; most fall along with the things that raised them, crushed by what once lifted them up.
items.core_idea: What lifts us up can also crush us

items.plain: No wall can keep Fortune out, so let us strengthen our defences within. If the inner self is safe, a person can be attacked but never captured.
items.core_idea: A secure inner self can't be captured

items.plain: Virtue fills the whole soul and is enough on its own. Losing children or friends makes no one less just or wise; while your virtue is unharmed, you will not feel the loss of what is taken.
items.core_idea: With virtue intact, no loss truly diminishes you

items.plain: A circle's size doesn't change its shape, and what is straight isn't judged by length or duration. Cut an honourable life down from a hundred years to a single day, and it is just as honourable.
items.core_idea: An honourable life is honourable at any length

items.plain: Virtue may rule kingdoms or be hemmed in by poverty, exile or bereavement, yet it is no smaller in a tiny corner. Happiness lives only in the mind, and needs knowledge of things divine and human.
items.core_idea: Virtue and happiness stay whole in narrow circumstances

items.plain: As the body shows signs before illness, a weak spirit trembles at troubles long before they come. It is madness to be tortured by the future instead of saving strength; if you can't escape suffering, at least postpone it.
items.core_idea: Don't suffer in advance from troubles not yet here

items.plain: No one should be tormented by the future, or by sorrows long past. Past and future are both absent; we feel neither of them, and there can be no pain except from what you actually feel.
items.core_idea: Past and future are absent; we feel neither

items.plain: Say what you feel and feel what you say; let your speech match your life. A person keeps his promise when he is the same whether you see him or hear him.
items.core_idea: Let your words match your life

items.plain: When will you learn it all, fix it in mind, and practise it? Memorising these truths is not enough; they must be tested. The happy person is not the one who knows them but the one who does them.
items.core_idea: Happiness comes from doing, not merely knowing

items.plain: We hurry toward virtue while weighed down by vices, and, shamefully, give what is honourable only our spare time. Yet what a reward awaits us if we break away from the distractions and evils that cling to us.
items.core_idea: We give virtue only our spare time

items.plain: If we climb out of these low depths, peace of mind and complete freedom await. That freedom means fearing neither people nor gods, craving neither wickedness nor excess, and having full power over yourself; being your own master is priceless.
items.core_idea: True freedom is mastery over oneself

fix.display_text: There await us, if ever we escape from these low dregs to that sublime and lofty height, peace of mind and, when all error has been driven out, perfect liberty. You ask what this freedom is? It means not fearing either men or gods; it means not craving wickedness or excess; it means possessing supreme power over oneself. And it is a priceless good to be master of oneself.

items.plain: You should keep learning as long as you don't know, even to the end of your life; as the proverb says, as long as you live, keep learning how to live. Even an old man should keep learning.
items.core_idea: Keep learning how to live as long as you live

items.plain: You will make as much progress as you try to make, so why wait? Money, titles and influence may come by chance, but wisdom and virtue never do; they take real effort, and the effort is worth it.
items.core_idea: Virtue never comes by chance; it takes effort

items.plain: Every action in life turns on whether it is honourable or shameful. A good person does what is honourable even if it brings toil, harm or danger, and refuses what is shameful even if it brings money, pleasure or power.
items.core_idea: A good person chooses honour over gain or safety

items.plain: Riches and honours don't make anyone great; you are measuring the pedestal along with the man. To learn someone's true worth, strip away wealth, titles and even the body, and look at the soul itself.
items.core_idea: Judge a person by the soul, not the pedestal

items.plain: A trouble thought about in advance strikes gently; for the unprepared, much of the pain is surprise. So the wise person gets used to future hardships by reflecting on them, knowing that anything may come.
items.core_idea: Troubles foreseen strike more gently

items.plain: Everyone knows they must die, yet they tremble when death nears. Weeping because you won't be alive a thousand years from now is as foolish as weeping because you weren't alive a thousand years ago.
items.core_idea: Not existing after death is like not existing before birth

items.plain: During a long illness I was often tempted to end my life, but thinking of my kind old father held me back: he could not bear to lose me. So I ordered myself to live. Sometimes even living takes courage.
items.core_idea: Sometimes it takes courage simply to live

items.plain: Honourable comfort heals, and whatever lifts the soul also helps the body. My studies saved me; I credit philosophy with my recovery and owe it my life, which is the least of what I owe it.
items.core_idea: Philosophy lifted the soul and healed the body

items.plain: My friends helped me recover with cheering words and hours at my bedside. Nothing helps the sick or removes the fear of death like friends' affection; I felt I would live on through them.
items.core_idea: Friends' love eases illness and the fear of death

items.plain: Illness has often put off death, and facing death has saved many. You will die not because you are sick but because you are alive; when you recover, you have escaped illness, not death.
items.core_idea: We die because we live, not because we are ill

items.plain: No one can suffer both severely and for long; Nature, who loves us tenderly, has made pain either bearable or short.
items.core_idea: Pain is either bearable or brief

items.plain: People say giving up usual pleasures, fasting and going hungry, is hard. It is at first, but then desire fades and the appetite tires. There is no bitterness in going without what you no longer want.
items.core_idea: Doing without is painless once desire fades

items.plain: Don't make your troubles heavier by complaining. Pain is slight if opinion adds nothing to it; tell yourself it is small and will pass, and you make it small. Everything depends on opinion; we suffer according to what we think.
items.core_idea: We suffer according to our opinion of things

items.plain: A person is as wretched as he convinces himself he is. Past sufferings, even if real, are over; what was bitter to bear is pleasant to have borne. Root out both fear of future pain and memory of past pain.
items.core_idea: Let go of past pain and fear of future pain

items.plain: In the middle of troubles, tell yourself that some day the memory of this sorrow may even bring you pleasure.
items.core_idea: Today's sorrow may one day be a pleasant memory

items.plain: Remember the honourable or brave things you have done and look at the good side of your own life. Go over in your mind the things you have most admired.
items.core_idea: Recall your good deeds and what you admire

items.plain: There is room for virtue even on a sickbed; you can be brave in your blankets, not only in battle. Your task is to wrestle bravely with illness. Be your own spectator and give yourself the applause.
items.core_idea: Bravery is possible even on a sickbed

items.plain: Hold this thought tightly: don't give in to hard times, don't trust good times, and keep in view everything Fortune could do, as if she surely will. What you have long expected arrives more gently.
items.core_idea: What is long expected arrives more gently

items.plain: Fame is the shadow of virtue and follows it even unwanted. Like a shadow, it sometimes goes ahead and sometimes lags behind, and when it comes late, after envy has retreated, it is all the greater.
items.core_idea: Fame follows virtue like a shadow, sometimes late

items.plain: Virtue is never lost for good; a day will reveal it. Whoever thinks only of his own generation lives for a few. Look to the countless people to come, who will judge you fairly, even if you never know it.
items.core_idea: Live for the fair judgement of future generations

items.plain: Virtue always rewards those who follow it faithfully and stay the same whether watched or caught unprepared. Pretence achieves nothing; masks are easily seen through, and lies are thin and transparent.
items.core_idea: Pretence fails; lies are thin and transparent

items.plain: If the body can be trained to take blows and scorching heat, how much more easily can the mind be toughened to take Fortune's blows and rise again? Virtue costs nothing; all that makes you good lies within you.
items.core_idea: Everything needed to be good lies within you

items.plain: Compare the faces of the poor and the rich to see how little evil poverty holds. The poor smile more often and more truly, their worries passing like clouds; the rich fake cheer while hiding festering sorrows.
items.core_idea: The poor often smile more truly than the rich

items.plain: To judge your own worth, set aside your money, property and honours, and look into your soul. Right now you are taking other people's word for who you are.
items.core_idea: Judge yourself by your soul, not others' opinion

items.plain: You complain of meeting an ungrateful person. Being wary only makes you stingy, so the good you might do is lost to you. Better to get nothing back than give nothing; after a poor crop, sow again.
items.core_idea: Better no return than never giving at all

items.plain: Finding one grateful person is worth risking many ungrateful ones; givers are often deceived, yet sailors return to sea after shipwreck. Dropping everything troublesome would make life dull; when the outcome is uncertain, keep trying until you succeed.
items.core_idea: Keep giving and trying despite disappointments

items.plain: A modest sum given at the right moment can do more than a fortune spent on a palace. It matters greatly whether a gift merely helps or truly rescues someone; often the gift is small but its effects are great.
items.core_idea: A small timely gift can matter greatly

items.plain: We should be as grateful as we can, because gratitude benefits ourselves. Whoever helps another helps himself, not because of any return, but because every virtue is its own reward. The payment for a good deed is having done it.
items.core_idea: The reward of a good deed is doing it

items.plain: When we do wrong, the worst of it stays with us; as Attalus said, evil drinks most of its own poison. The ungrateful person torments himself, forgetting kindnesses and clinging to injuries, and nothing is more wretched.
items.core_idea: Evil drinks most of its own poison

items.plain: Bad people enjoy a gift only while receiving it, but the wise person delights in having received it, a joy that never fades. He looks down on wrongs done to him and forgets them, not by accident but by choice.
items.core_idea: Remember kindnesses; choose to forget wrongs

items.plain: We value a favour most while seeking it and least once we have it, because greed for more makes us forget. Riches, titles and power are not praised because they're worth wanting, but wanted because they're praised.
items.core_idea: Things are wanted because praised, not praised because worthy

items.plain: Both frantic busyness and idleness are to be avoided. Someone lounging on a perfumed couch is as good as dead; leisure without study is death, a tomb for the living.
items.core_idea: Leisure without study is a living tomb

items.plain: What good is retreating from the world when the real causes of worry follow you across the sea? No hiding place keeps out fear of death or pain; troubles press in from outside, and fret within even in solitude.
items.core_idea: Our anxieties follow us wherever we hide

items.plain: We don't praise poverty, exile, pain or death; we praise the person whom poverty can't humble, who goes into exile with dignity, whom pain can't force, and whose soul death takes before it can be thrown into confusion.
items.core_idea: We praise those hardship cannot break, not hardship

items.plain: Death is not truly an evil, but it looks like one. We are made to love our existence, death seems to rob us of familiar goods, and we shrink from an unknown future and the world of shades.
items.core_idea: Death only seems evil because we fear the unknown

items.plain: No act is honourable unless you give yourself to it wholeheartedly. If you act from fear of worse or hope of gain, you are torn two ways and the glory is gone; virtue acts with an undivided, fearless spirit.
items.core_idea: Honourable action needs a wholehearted, undivided spirit

items.plain: Live as if everyone could see you, and think as if someone could look into your soul, because someone can. Nothing is hidden from God; he witnesses our souls and enters our thoughts.
items.core_idea: Live as if God sees into your soul

items.plain: I will watch myself and review each day, a most useful habit. What makes us bad is that none of us looks back over our lives; we think only of what's next, yet our plans always depend on the past.
items.core_idea: Review each day; the future depends on the past

items.plain: A gap opens quickly between two people going different ways. My young slave is climbing up while I am coming down, and coming down is much faster. In fact, my life isn't descending now; it is falling.
items.core_idea: In old age, life falls faster than it rose

items.plain: The roar and cheering from the races surround me, but they don't break my train of thought. I bear the uproar calmly; the mass of voices sounds like crashing waves or wind in treetops, noise without meaning.
items.core_idea: A settled mind hears uproar as meaningless noise

items.plain: Drunkenness doesn't create vice; it reveals it by stripping away the shame that holds people back. Once wine takes over the mind, every hidden evil comes out: the lustful, arrogant, cruel and spiteful all give their vices free rein.
items.core_idea: Drunkenness doesn't create vice; it reveals it

items.plain: What glory is there in out-drinking everyone? When the others are asleep or vomiting and you alone are left standing as champion, you have still been beaten by the barrel.
items.core_idea: Winning at drinking means being beaten by drink

items.plain: If you come to resemble someone you admire deeply, resemble him as a child resembles a father, not as a painting resembles its subject, for a painting is lifeless.
items.core_idea: Imitate like a living child, not a lifeless copy

items.plain: Whatever stands out in human affairs, however petty, is reached by a hard, steep road. But the peak of true greatness, far above Fortune, from which you look down on all that seems loftiest, is reached over level ground.
items.core_idea: True greatness lies above Fortune, along a level road

items.plain: Animals, wild or tame, don't obey reason, and neither do passions, however mild. Tigers and lions only soften their wildness for a while, then turn savage when you least expect it. Vices are never truly tamed.
items.core_idea: Vices are never truly tamed

items.plain: It's foolish to think you can control how something ends when you couldn't control how it started. It is easier to keep a thing out than to hold it down once you've let it in.
items.core_idea: Easier to keep out than to control once in

items.plain: Being full is the limit of eating and drinking: one eats more, another less, but both are satisfied. So too, one lives many years and another few; it doesn't matter, if the many held as much happiness as the few.
items.core_idea: A short happy life equals a long one

items.plain: Evil is giving in to so-called evils and handing them your freedom. Bravery is not recklessness or love of danger; it is knowing what is truly evil and what isn't, and patiently bearing what only seems evil.
items.core_idea: Bravery is knowing what is truly evil

items.plain: A pilot promises not a smooth voyage but skilled steering, and storms show his skill all the more. If the sea sinks him only on an even keel, he has done his job; storms affect his success, not his work.
items.core_idea: Storms affect your success, not your skill

items.plain: Phidias could make the best possible statue from ivory, bronze, marble or cheaper stuff. So the wise person practises virtue in wealth or poverty, home or exile, health or frailty, making something worthwhile of whatever fortune brings.
items.core_idea: Make something worthwhile of whatever fortune gives

items.plain: If I have bread, figs are a treat; if not, figs are my bread, so every day is a feast. The soul is greatest when it drops all outside things, finding peace by fearing nothing and riches by craving none.
items.core_idea: Riches come from craving no riches

items.plain: I ride a shabby farm cart and can hardly bear others thinking it mine; I blush when grander travellers pass. So the simplicity I praise hasn't fully taken root. Whoever blushes at a rattletrap will boast in a fine carriage.
items.core_idea: Shame at simplicity reveals hidden vanity

items.plain: You call a man rich for his gold plate, his lands everywhere and his huge account books. But he is poor, because he is in debt for everything he has, whether he borrowed from a person or from Fortune.
items.core_idea: Everything we own is borrowed from Fortune

items.plain: The highest good lives in the soul, and unless the soul is pure and holy, there is no room in it for God.
items.core_idea: Only a pure soul has room for God

items.plain: The worst punishment for a crime lies in the crime itself. Don't think punishment waits for the hangman or prison; it comes the moment the crime is committed.
items.core_idea: Wrongdoing is its own immediate punishment

items.plain: True goods give confidence and greatness of soul, but riches give shamelessness and arrogance, and arrogance is only a fake show of greatness.
items.core_idea: Arrogance is a false show of greatness

items.plain: Why study where Ulysses wandered instead of how to keep ourselves from going astray? We face storms of the spirit daily. Show me instead how to love my country, wife and father, and sail toward them even after shipwreck.
items.core_idea: Study to live well, not for idle trivia

items.plain: You teach me how high and low notes make harmony; instead, bring my soul into harmony with itself. You show me the mournful keys; show me rather how to avoid a mournful note in hard times.
items.core_idea: Seek harmony in the soul, not just in music

items.plain: What use is dividing land if I can't share it with my brother, or am bitter when a neighbour takes a scrap? The mathematician teaches me to lose none of my boundaries; I want to lose them all lightly.
items.core_idea: Learn to lose possessions with a light heart

items.plain: I don't know what will happen, but I know what could, so I await the whole future without misgiving. Knowing anything can happen but not everything will, I am ready for good and prepared for bad.
items.core_idea: Be ready for good, prepared for bad

items.plain: Temperance governs our desires, driving some out and bringing others back to a healthy level. It knows the right measure of appetite is not what you want to take, but what you ought to take.
items.core_idea: Take what you ought, not what you want

items.plain: Kindness forbids being overbearing or grasping, and is gentle and courteous to everyone in word, deed and feeling. It treats no misfortune as only someone else's, and values its own good because one day it will be another's.
items.core_idea: Kindness treats no one's trouble as only theirs

items.plain: We spend huge amounts of time and bore others to earn the praise "What a learned man you are!" Let us be content with a plainer compliment: "What a good man you are!"
items.core_idea: Better to be called good than learned

items.plain: Knowing the worth of things, knowing when to act, and restraining impulse are three different skills. Life is in harmony only when action follows impulse, and impulse is as strong as its object is truly worth seeking.
items.core_idea: Let impulse match the true worth of things

items.plain: Medicine starts helping when its touch makes the sick body sting. I will say things that help people against their will. Let words other than compliments reach you; if you won't hear the truth alone, hear it together.
items.core_idea: Helpful truth may sting like medicine

items.plain: What good are your many bedrooms? You sleep in only one. No place is truly yours where you yourself are not.
items.core_idea: You can only be in one place at once

items.plain: Study not to add to what you know, but to make what you know better.
items.core_idea: Study to improve knowledge, not just add to it

items.plain: How can you admire both Daedalus, who invented the saw, and Diogenes, who, seeing a boy drink from his hand, smashed his own cup as needless baggage and curled up in his tub? Which one is wise?
items.core_idea: Wisdom lies in needing less, not inventing more

items.plain: Nature didn't make humans alone unable to live without contrivances; shelter and food were ready, free and easily got. We made life hard by scorning what is easy and making things precious and admired.
items.core_idea: Nature gave enough; we made life difficult

items.plain: The wise person has discovered truth and nature, seeing the divine in it, and taught us to follow the gods and accept chance as their command. He showed that the happiest need no happiness, and the most powerful rule themselves.
items.core_idea: Most powerful is the one who rules himself

items.plain: Greed brought poverty into the world, and by craving much it lost everything.
items.core_idea: Greed creates poverty by craving too much

items.plain: Nature does not hand out virtue; becoming good is a skill you have to learn.
items.core_idea: Goodness is learned, not given by nature

items.plain: A soul gets virtue only by being trained, taught and perfected through constant practice. We are born to pursue it, not already holding it; even the best people, before instruction, have only the raw material of virtue, not virtue itself.
items.core_idea: We are born able to gain virtue, not with it

items.plain: Surprise makes disasters heavier, and everyone hurts more from what catches them off guard. So nothing should be unexpected: send your mind ahead to meet every problem, thinking not of what usually happens but of what can happen.
items.core_idea: Expect what can happen, not just what usually does

items.plain: What long years, great toil and the gods' kindness built can be scattered in a day, even an instant. It would comfort us if things perished as slowly as they grow, but growth is slow and ruin is fast.
items.core_idea: Growth is slow, but ruin is swift

items.plain: A setback has often made room for better fortune, and many buildings have fallen only to rise higher.
items.core_idea: Setbacks often make room for something better

items.plain: Don't judge people's worth by their graves or the monuments of different sizes along the road; their ashes make everyone level. We are unequal at birth but equal in death.
items.core_idea: Unequal at birth, equal in death

items.plain: Nature says the hardships you complain of are the same for all; she can make nothing easier, but anyone can make things easier for himself through equanimity. You must suffer pain, hunger, old age, sickness, loss and death.
items.core_idea: Equanimity eases the hardships everyone must face

items.plain: How crazy it is to fear a bad reputation among people who themselves have bad reputations.
items.core_idea: Don't fear the judgement of the disreputable

items.plain: The happy person is the one nothing can weaken; he stays on the heights relying on no one but himself, because anyone who leans on a prop may fall.
items.core_idea: Lean on no prop and you cannot fall

items.plain: The happy life is peace of mind and lasting calm, which come from greatness of soul and firm good judgement. You reach it by seeing the whole truth and acting always with order, measure, fitness and a kindly, reasonable will.
items.core_idea: The happy life is lasting peace of mind

items.plain: Nature has wrapped the soul in the body like a cloak. But no one judges clothes by the wardrobe that holds them, and the scabbard doesn't make the sword good or bad.
items.core_idea: The body is only the soul's cloak

items.plain: Clouds don't shrink the sun; it keeps its course and shines out undiminished. Likewise, obstacles take nothing from virtue, though it may look dimmer to us. Disasters, losses and wrongs affect virtue only as a cloud affects the sun.
items.core_idea: Hardships hide virtue like clouds hide the sun

items.plain: The heart of virtue is needing no day beyond today and not counting the days you have; in the briefest moment, virtue completes an eternity of good.
items.core_idea: Virtue needs nothing beyond the present moment

items.plain: The soul knows that true riches are kept somewhere other than piled-up treasure houses: it is the soul, not the strongbox, that should be filled.
items.core_idea: Fill the soul, not the strongbox

items.plain: Why does it matter how soon you leave a place you must leave anyway? Aim to live rightly, not long: long life needs only Fate, right living needs the soul. A life is long if it is full, through self-mastery.
items.core_idea: Live rightly rather than long

items.plain: Let our lives be like precious jewels, valued not for their size but for their weight. Measure them by what they achieve, not by how long they last.
items.core_idea: Measure life by its weight, not its length

items.plain: A short life can be a complete life, as a short person can be a complete person. How long I exist isn't mine to decide, but how I live is. I must stop drifting in darkness and truly live.
items.core_idea: How long you live isn't yours; how you live is

items.plain: Death comes to everyone; the killer soon follows the killed. It is a small thing that people worry about so much. And what does it matter how long you avoid what you cannot escape?
items.core_idea: Death comes to all; delay matters little

items.plain: Remember that pain has an excellent quality: if it lasts long it can't be severe, and if it is severe it can't last long. We should bravely accept whatever the unchanging laws of the universe demand of us.
items.core_idea: Severe pain is short; long pain is mild

items.plain: The soul holds the seed of everything honourable, and advice stirs it to grow, as a gentle breeze fans a spark into flame. A touch, a jolt, is enough to rouse virtue.
items.core_idea: Good advice fans the seed of virtue within

items.plain: Nothing improves the mind or steadies a wavering spirit like spending time with good people. Seeing and hearing them gradually sinks into the heart; meeting wise people lifts us, and a great person can help even in silence.
items.core_idea: Good company slowly shapes the heart

items.plain: Virtue comes partly from training and partly from practice: first learn, then strengthen what you've learned by acting on it.
items.core_idea: Learn first, then strengthen learning by action

items.plain: Every word we hear does some harm, whether curses or good wishes. Enemies' prayers plant false fears, and friends' kind wishes spoil us, sending us after distant, uncertain goods when happiness is in store at home.
items.core_idea: Happiness is found at home, not in distant goods

items.plain: Don't envy those the crowd calls great, or let applause or a magistrate in purple disturb your calm; he is no happier than you. For a command that helps you and harms no one, clear away your own faults.
items.core_idea: Master your own faults rather than envy power

items.plain: Never believe that anyone can become happy through someone else's unhappiness.
items.core_idea: No one gains happiness from another's misery

items.plain: A large part of health is having left behind those who advise madness and having fled far from company that harms everyone in it.
items.core_idea: Leaving harmful company is part of health

items.plain: Stop showing off and you'll stop craving. Ambition, luxury and self-indulgence need a stage to perform on; withdraw from the crowd and you cure them all.
items.core_idea: Without an audience, craving fades

items.plain: Good fortune and good sense sit at opposite poles, which is why we are wiser in hard times. It is prosperity that takes away our goodness.
items.core_idea: Adversity makes us wiser; prosperity corrupts

items.plain: We often want one thing and pray for another, not telling the truth even to the gods, who either don't listen or take pity on us.
items.core_idea: We aren't honest even in our prayers

items.plain: We honour those who sit by a sick friend's bed, but those hoping for an inheritance are vultures waiting for carrion. The same act can be shameful or honourable; purpose and manner make all the difference.
items.core_idea: Purpose makes the same act honourable or shameful

items.plain: As our beliefs are, so will our actions and thoughts be; and as our actions and thoughts are, so will our lives be.
items.core_idea: Beliefs shape actions, and actions shape lives

items.plain: Life without ideals wanders aimlessly, and setting up an ideal requires principles. Nothing is more shameful than uncertain, wavering conduct and the habit of timidly backing away.
items.core_idea: Without ideals, life wavers shamefully

items.plain: Do you want to win the gods' favour? Then be a good person. Whoever imitates the gods worships them enough.
items.core_idea: Be good: imitating the gods is worship

items.plain: How small a thing it is merely not to harm someone you ought to help! What truly deserves praise is when people treat each other with kindness.
items.core_idea: Not harming is little; kindness deserves praise

items.plain: Nature made us kin, from one source for one end, and gave us affection and a bent for friendship. By her law, doing wrong is worse than suffering it. Let our hands be ready to help wherever help is needed.
items.core_idea: We are kin; doing wrong is worse than suffering it

items.plain: Keep this in your heart: I am human, and nothing human is foreign to me. Let us share things, since we share birth. We are like the stones of an arch, which would fall without each other's support.
items.core_idea: We hold each other up like stones in an arch

items.plain: Let us ignore gossip and value each thing by asking what it actually is, not what it is called.
items.core_idea: Judge things by what they are, not their name

items.plain: Only those with a fixed standard of judgement have peace of mind; others drift back and forth, rejecting then seeking the same things, because they judge by rumour. If you want to desire the same things always, desire the truth.
items.core_idea: To want steadily, want the truth

items.plain: Of all the evils you complain about, the only real one is your complaining. There is no misery for a person unless he thinks something miserable. The day I find anything unbearable, I won't be able to bear myself.
items.core_idea: Complaining is the only real evil

items.plain: I am ill, but that is part of my lot. My slaves are sick, my income is gone, my house is falling apart, and I have faced losses, accidents, work and fear. This is common; in fact, it is unavoidable.
items.core_idea: Troubles are a common, unavoidable part of life

items.plain: When things go hard, I have trained myself not just to obey God but to agree with Him, willingly. Everything that makes us groan is part of the tax of life, which you should never hope to escape.
items.core_idea: Hardships are life's tax; pay it willingly

items.plain: A long life includes all these troubles, just as a long journey includes dust, mud and rain.
items.core_idea: Long lives bring troubles, like mud on journeys

items.plain: Life is a battle. Those who brave the sea, steep crags and dangerous campaigns are heroes in the front ranks; those in rotten luxury while others toil are turtle-doves, safe only because people despise them.
items.core_idea: Life is a battle; idle luxury is contemptible

items.plain: You are wrong to think luxury, bad manners and other vices each generation blames on its age are special to our time. They are the vices of humanity, not of the era; no age has been free of blame.
items.core_idea: Vices belong to humanity, not to any age

items.plain: We slide into wrongdoing easily, with or without guides and companions. The road to vice is downhill and steep, and many become incurable because, unlike mistakes in a craft, the mistakes of life bring pleasure.
items.core_idea: The road to vice is steep and pleasant

items.plain: A good conscience wants to come out and be seen, but wickedness is afraid even of shadows.
items.core_idea: A good conscience seeks light; guilt fears shadows

items.plain: Good luck saves many from punishment, but no one from fear, because we loathe what Nature condemns. Those who hide their wrongs can never be sure of staying hidden; their conscience convicts them. Guilt always lives in fear.
items.core_idea: Guilt may escape punishment but never fear

items.plain: No one who depends on good fortune is happy; joy from outside will leave, but joy springing from yourself is sound and lasts. Outside things can please and serve, but only if they depend on us, not we on them.
items.core_idea: Joy from within lasts; joy from outside leaves

items.plain: Fortune's gifts are good only if their owner masters himself, not his possessions him. Fortune gives no good or evil, only raw material; the soul, stronger than any fortune, shapes it into a happy or wretched life.
items.core_idea: The soul, not Fortune, makes life happy or wretched

items.plain: A bad person makes everything bad, even what arrived looking best. A good and honest person corrects Fortune's wrongs, softens hardship by knowing how to bear it, enjoys prosperity gratefully and moderately, and faces trouble steadily and bravely.
items.core_idea: A good person turns hardship to good

items.plain: Whenever things go against your expectations, say to yourself, as a braver and truer phrase to steady your spirit, that heaven decided on something better.
items.core_idea: When plans fail, trust that heaven chose better

items.plain: It is tragic for the soul to dread the future, anxious to keep its pleasures to the end. Such a soul never rests and loses the present. Fearing to lose something is no different from grieving its loss.
items.core_idea: Fearing loss is as painful as loss itself

items.plain: Foresee and avoid the harm you can, helped by confidence and a mind resolved to endure anything. Whoever can bear Fortune can guard against it. Nothing is more foolish than fearing trouble before it comes.
items.core_idea: Prepare for trouble, but don't fear it early

items.plain: What you are called owner of is in your hands but not truly yours. We must lose our lives as surely as our property, and knowing this is a comfort. Lose things calmly, since you must lose life too.
items.core_idea: Lose things calmly; even life must be lost

items.plain: Facing loss, remember what you've lost and don't let its enjoyment vanish with it. Having can be taken away; having had, never. Chance takes the thing but leaves its enjoyment, unless we throw that away by regretting.
items.core_idea: Having can be taken, but having had cannot

items.plain: Why lose heart? What could be done can be done, if we purify our souls and follow Nature; straying from it enslaves us to chance. Return to our true state, and we can endure pain and defy Fortune.
items.core_idea: Follow Nature and Fortune cannot conquer you

items.plain: If you had lost a friend, the greatest blow of all, you should have tried to rejoice that you had him rather than mourn that you lost him.
items.core_idea: Rejoice in having had a friend, not only mourn

items.plain: Do you bury the friendship with the friend? Were those years of closeness for nothing? Much of those we loved stays with us after they are gone. The past is ours, and nothing is more secure than what has been.
items.core_idea: The past we shared with loved ones stays ours

items.plain: We are ungrateful for past joys because we hope for the future, which soon becomes past anyway. Enjoying only the present limits us; the future delights by anticipation and the past by memory, but only the past is certain.
items.core_idea: Past joys are certain; cherish them

items.plain: See how swiftly time runs, with all humanity rushing to the same point only moments apart. The one you think has passed away has only gone on ahead. Why mourn the one before you when you travel the same road?
items.core_idea: The dead have only gone ahead on our road

items.plain: Whoever complains that someone died is complaining that he was human. Everyone shares the same terms: whoever is given birth is bound to die.
items.core_idea: To be born is to be bound to die

items.plain: Time separates us, but death makes us equal. Life's span is uncertain and everything shifts at Fortune's command; only death is sure. Yet everyone complains about the one thing in which no one is deceived.
items.core_idea: Amid all uncertainty, only death is sure

items.plain: Life itself is neither good nor bad; it is simply the place where good and bad happen.
items.core_idea: Life is the place where good and evil happen

items.plain: Some feelings claim their rights: tears fall despite us, and shedding them eases the soul. Let them fall, but don't force them; weep as feeling moves you, not as imitation demands, and add nothing to natural grief.
items.core_idea: Let tears fall naturally, without adding to grief
